prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and timely topic: the conceptual instability of “sentiment” in sentiment analysis, especially as SA systems are increasingly deployed in socially consequential domains such as healthcare, policy, and finance. The paper’s central claim—that the field often operationalizes sentiment without sufficiently explicit definitions, interdisciplinary grounding, or transparency about measurement choices—is compelling and, in broad strokes, correct. The paper also usefully connects this conceptual issue to downstream concerns about bias, opacity, and misuse, and it proposes an ethics-sheet style intervention intended to improve documentation and reflection. Overall, I found the paper thought-provoking and potentially valuable as a critical survey for the NLP/ML community. At the same time, the paper currently falls short of the methodological rigor and precision needed for a top-tier venue. Its strongest contribution is agenda-setting; its weakest aspects are the survey methodology, evidentiary standards for several claims, and the novelty/validation of the proposed ethics sheet.

The paper’s main strengths are threefold. First, it addresses a real blind spot in the literature. Much SA work does indeed conflate sentiment, opinion, emotion, affect, subjectivity, stance, and polarity, and the paper is right to emphasize that these are not interchangeable constructs. The discussion in Sections 3 and 5 is especially useful in surfacing this conceptual slippage and in arguing that such slippage matters more when SA is embedded in sociotechnical systems rather than used as a narrow benchmark task. Second, the paper attempts to synthesize technical SA literature with perspectives from psychology, sociology, and linguistics. Even if the interdisciplinary treatment is somewhat uneven, the effort itself is valuable and aligns with growing interest in construct validity, measurement, and sociotechnical evaluation in NLP. Third, the paper’s normative recommendations are sensible: explicit task definitions, documentation of intended use, transparency about data and code, and bias testing are all good practices. The ethics-sheet framing may be practically useful for practitioners, especially outside core NLP.

That said, the paper has substantial weaknesses in methodology and framing that limit confidence in its conclusions. The biggest issue is that this is presented as a survey of 189 papers, but the paper does not provide enough methodological detail to assess the validity, reproducibility, or representativeness of the survey. The search strategy is only loosely described, inclusion/exclusion criteria are underspecified, and the coding protocol is not sufficiently formalized. For example, the paper states that it collected papers from SCOPUS, Semantic Scholar, ACL Anthology, NeurIPS, AAAI, and ACM using targeted keywords, but it does not clearly specify exact queries, date ranges, screening stages, deduplication procedures, or how “peer-reviewed” was operationalized across sources. It is also unclear how the 189 papers were sampled relative to the much larger SA literature, and whether the sample is intended to be representative or illustrative. The limitations section acknowledges non-exhaustiveness, but that does not fully resolve the problem because many of the paper’s quantitative claims are stated in a way that invites generalization to the field as a whole.

Relatedly, the qualitative coding process needs much stronger documentation. The paper says that multiple authors iteratively classified papers and verified coding, but it does not define the annotation schema precisely enough. What counted as “explicitly defining sentiment”? What counted as “explaining the employed framework”? How were borderline cases handled? Were papers allowed multiple labels for application domains? Was inter-annotator agreement measured? Without agreement statistics or at least a detailed codebook, the reported counts—such as “very few works (<5%) explicitly define sentiment”—are difficult to evaluate. This is especially important because the paper’s central thesis depends on these coding judgments. A more rigorous systematic review methodology, ideally PRISMA-like or at least clearly structured, would significantly strengthen the work.

A second major concern is that some of the paper’s conceptual claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The paper argues that SA lacks a “well-defined comprehensive framework” and that there is an “absence of synchronization” in the field. There is truth here, but the paper sometimes treats heterogeneity as inherently problematic without sufficiently distinguishing between harmful ambiguity and legitimate task variation. It is not obvious that all SA tasks should share a single standardized construct. Product-review polarity classification, financial tone analysis, emotion recognition, aspect-based sentiment analysis, and clinical narrative interpretation may reasonably require different operationalizations. The stronger and more defensible claim is not that the field needs one unified definition of sentiment, but that each task should clearly specify its target construct, intended use, and measurement assumptions. The paper gestures toward this position, but often slips into language suggesting that standardization itself is the solution. I would encourage the authors to sharpen this distinction. The problem is less pluralism per se than unacknowledged pluralism.

The interdisciplinary discussion is promising but somewhat underdeveloped and occasionally imprecise. Section 3.2 contrasts computational and “social” perceptions of sentiment, but the treatment of psychology, sociology, and linguistics is selective and sometimes conflates measurement modalities. For instance, the discussion of physiological indicators sits awkwardly beside text-based SA, since most NLP systems do not claim to infer physiological states directly. More importantly, the paper could benefit from a clearer construct-validity framing: what latent construct is each SA task trying to measure, what observable text signals are used as proxies, and under what assumptions is that mapping valid? This would provide a more principled bridge between social science concepts and NLP operationalizations than the current broader critique. As written, the interdisciplinary section is useful as motivation, but not yet analytically tight enough to ground the later empirical claims.

The analysis of applications in Section 4.1 is interesting, but again the evidentiary basis is thinner than it appears. The thematic categories are plausible, yet the paper does not report category frequencies in Table 3 despite saying the table includes them, and the figure is referenced but not numerically summarized in the text. More importantly, the claim that health/medicine and government/policy are especially prominent depends heavily on the sampling strategy. If the search terms included “applications,” the resulting corpus may overrepresent certain domains or review-style papers. The paper should be more careful to frame these findings as observations about the sampled corpus rather than definitive statements about the field.

Section 4.2 on “Sentiment Analysis as a Service” raises worthwhile concerns about accessibility and transparency, but the construction of this sample is also unclear. The paper mixes “models” and “datasets” in ways that are sometimes hard to follow, and the criterion of “publicly accessible for use as AIaaS” seems stretched. Many research models are not actually deployed services, and lack of code release is not equivalent to being an AIaaS black box. If the authors want to analyze SA as a service, they should focus on actual APIs, libraries, or hosted systems and evaluate them as such. If instead they want to analyze public research artifacts, then the framing should be about reproducibility and openness, not AIaaS. As written, the section conflates these categories. The accessibility statistics are still useful, but the conceptual framing needs correction.

The bias discussion in Section 4.3 is important and likely to resonate with the community, but it currently feels more illustrative than systematic. The TextBlob example is intuitive, yet it is a very limited demonstration and does not establish broader claims about SA systems in general. Since the paper already cites stronger prior work on demographic bias in sentiment systems, it would be better either to expand this section into a more systematic empirical audit across multiple representative models or to rely more explicitly on prior literature and present the TextBlob example as a toy illustration only. Also, the interpretation of negative sentiment scores as potentially being read as “toxic or hateful” should be stated more carefully; the issue is not that sentiment scores literally mean toxicity, but that downstream users may overinterpret them or use them in harmful pipelines. Precision in this section matters.

The proposed ethics sheet is a reasonable practical artifact, but its novelty relative to Mohammad (2022) and related documentation frameworks is somewhat limited. The paper acknowledges this prior work, but it is not fully clear what is substantively new here beyond adaptation to the authors’ survey findings. That could still be a valid contribution, but then the paper should position it as a domain-specific refinement and ideally validate it. For example, the authors could apply the ethics sheet retrospectively to a subset of surveyed papers and show what kinds of gaps it reveals, or conduct a small expert evaluation of whether the questions are useful, complete, and actionable. Without such validation, the ethics sheet reads more like a sensible checklist than a research contribution in its own right.

There are also several presentation and writing issues that should be addressed. The paper is generally readable, but there are many grammatical errors, awkward phrasings, and inconsistencies that reduce clarity. Some examples include missing words (“We conducted an analysis 60 papers”), duplicated or inconsistent terminology, and occasional overstatement. The paper would benefit from careful copyediting. Some tables are also not fully aligned with the text. Table 3 claims to include frequencies but does not show them. Table 2 mixes frameworks, definitions, and examples in a way that is somewhat ad hoc. The numbering of questions in the ethics sheet repeats Q3 and then uses Q3.1/Q3.2, which is awkward. These are fixable issues, but they matter for a survey paper where clarity and structure are central.

I also think the paper should engage more directly with adjacent concepts in NLP evaluation and measurement. In particular, the authors’ concerns are closely related to construct validity, dataset documentation, task formulation, and benchmark governance. Framing the paper partly through construct validity would help avoid the impression that the authors are simply asking for more definitions. The deeper issue is whether the labels and outputs used in SA correspond to the social phenomena that users think they measure. That framing would also connect the paper more strongly to broader ML methodology rather than only ethics.

For improvement, I would strongly recommend the following. First, substantially strengthen the survey methodology section. Provide exact search queries, databases, time windows, inclusion/exclusion criteria, deduplication procedures, and a screening flow diagram. Define the coding categories precisely and report inter-annotator agreement. Second, temper and sharpen the claims: distinguish clearly between the need for explicit construct specification and the stronger claim that the field should converge on a single standardized notion of sentiment. Third, clean up the “AIaaS” framing and separate openness/reproducibility analysis from service deployment analysis unless the sample truly consists of deployed services. Fourth, either expand the empirical bias audit into a more systematic experiment across several models or reduce the emphasis on the TextBlob example and rely on prior literature more carefully. Fifth, strengthen the ethics-sheet contribution by validating it, even modestly, through expert feedback or retrospective application. Sixth, improve the writing and consistency throughout.

In terms of significance, I think the paper addresses an important problem and could stimulate useful discussion, especially among researchers who treat SA as a generic plug-in component for downstream applications. Its core message—that sentiment is not a self-evident construct and that careless operationalization can produce misleading or harmful systems—is valuable. However, in its current form, the paper is more of a persuasive position/survey hybrid than a rigorous systematic review. For a top-tier ML/NLP venue, I would expect stronger methodological grounding and tighter empirical support.

My overall assessment is therefore mixed but leaning positive on importance and negative on readiness. I appreciate the ambition and agree with much of the critique, but I do not think the current version fully substantiates its strongest claims or cleanly separates evidence from advocacy. With substantial revision, this could become a strong critical survey or position paper. In its present form, I would be hesitant to recommend acceptance at a top-tier conference, though I do think the work has clear potential and addresses a topic the field should take seriously.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper presents a critical survey of 189 sentiment analysis (SA) papers spanning applications, models, datasets, surveys, and frameworks, with the central claim that SA lacks explicit, interdisciplinary definitions of “sentiment” despite being widely deployed in sociotechnical domains such as healthcare, policy, finance, and social media. The paper contrasts technical notions of sentiment used in NLP with psychological and sociological perspectives, reports descriptive statistics showing that few surveyed works explicitly define sentiment or their sentiment framework, discusses heterogeneity in sentiment metrics and limited transparency of public SA systems, illustrates bias via a small TextBlob example and prior literature, and proposes recommendations plus an ethics sheet intended to guide more responsible SA development and deployment.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: the conceptual mismatch between NLP sentiment analysis practice and the social/psychological complexity of sentiment.
Takes a broad sociotechnical perspective rather than focusing only on model performance, which is valuable for the community.
Surveys a relatively large body of literature (189 papers) across applications, models, datasets, and surveys, giving the paper potentially useful breadth.
Highlights concrete concerns around definitional ambiguity, metric heterogeneity, transparency, and bias in deployed SA systems.
The proposed ethics-sheet style checklist is practical and may be useful for practitioners and reviewers as a lightweight governance tool.
The paper is well motivated by real-world deployment contexts such as healthcare and policymaking, where simplistic polarity labels can be problematic.
weaknesses: The survey methodology is insufficiently rigorous and reproducible for a paper making strong quantitative claims about the field; search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, coding protocol, and inter-annotator agreement are under-specified.

Many conclusions are based on descriptive counts without a clear operational definition of what qualifies as a “definition,” “framework,” or “application,” making the reported percentages hard to validate.
The paper often conflates lack of standardization with scientific invalidity; diversity of task formulations in SA may reflect legitimate differences in application goals rather than a flaw per se.

The empirical support for harms is weak within the paper itself: the TextBlob demonstration is anecdotal, uses a tiny hand-crafted set of examples, and does not establish prevalence, causality, or downstream impact.
The proposed ethics sheet is sensible but not clearly novel relative to Mohammad (2022) and related datasheets/model cards work; the paper does not evaluate whether the checklist improves practice.
The argument occasionally overgeneralizes from selected examples to the entire SA field, including claims about black-box behavior, lack of social comprehension, and undermined research integrity.

There is limited engagement with counterexamples or more nuanced SA subfields (e.g., structured sentiment, emotion analysis, domain-specific lexicons, contextual and aspect-based methods) that already acknowledge task distinctions.
The paper does not clearly separate criticism of sentiment analysis as a construct from criticism of specific datasets/models/deployment practices, which weakens the precision of its claims.
methodological_flaws: Sampling and corpus construction are not sufficiently specified. The paper states that papers were gathered from multiple sources using targeted keywords and then filtered, but does not provide a reproducible protocol, exact queries, date ranges, deduplication rules, or a PRISMA-style accounting. This undermines the validity of all quantitative survey findings.

The thematic analysis for applications lacks methodological detail and reliability statistics. Although the paper says multiple authors classified papers recursively, it does not report annotation guidelines, adjudication procedures, or inter-rater agreement (e.g., Cohen’s kappa), so category assignments may be subjective.

Key constructs are operationalized ambiguously. For example, counting whether a paper ‘defines sentiment’ or ‘defines the SA framework’ depends heavily on subjective judgment, yet no coding rubric is provided. Therefore claims such as ‘<5% define sentiment’ are not scientifically well supported.

The accessibility analysis of 43 models mixes heterogeneous artifacts (papers, models, services, repositories) and uses unclear criteria for ‘publicly available,’ ‘ease of access,’ and ‘black box.’ Lack of released code or data does not by itself imply AIaaS deployment or black-box sociotechnical risk in the way claimed.

The metric analysis is conceptually muddled. The paper groups diverse label spaces (polarity, emotions, VAD dimensions, subjectivity) under ‘sentiment metrics’ and then argues they are inconsistent, but these often correspond to different tasks rather than incompatible measurements of the same latent variable.

The statement clarifying that ‘sentiment regression’ refers to ‘regression to the mean techniques applied in measurement’ is scientifically incorrect or at least highly confused terminology. Mapping text to a continuous sentiment score is not ‘regression to the mean’; this misuse weakens the methodological credibility of the analysis.

The TextBlob bias experiment is not a valid empirical study. It uses a handful of manually chosen prompts, no baseline, no statistical analysis, no robustness checks, and no comparison across models or contexts. It can illustrate a concern but cannot substantiate broad claims about SA harms.

Several causal inferences are overstated. For instance, the paper suggests that absent definitions or heterogeneous frameworks directly cause sociodemographic bias, but no evidence is provided isolating this mechanism from dataset imbalance, annotation artifacts, model architecture, or deployment context.

The paper argues for standardization of sentiment measures, yet its own interdisciplinary review emphasizes that sentiment, opinion, emotion, and subjectivity are distinct constructs. This creates a tension in scientific logic: if tasks are genuinely different, forcing standardization may be inappropriate; what is needed may be clearer task specification rather than unified measurement.

Novelty claims around the ethics sheet are limited because a closely related ethics sheet for emotion recognition and sentiment analysis already exists (Mohammad, 2022), and the paper does not provide comparative analysis or validation showing what is substantively new or more effective here.
